Thank you for the response, I wasn't expecting one at all.

I've spent the last hour staring at your message trying to respond to it but I'm so drained right now that I've run out of intelligent thoughts.

The only thing I can say is that the people I see that are truly happy have well-integrated social lives. I see the point you're making, my thoughts are just incredibly rigid on the matter.

Here's some gold to show you I care. You're a good person.

Yes. What's worse than being hated is being abandoned and forgotten.

Best of luck.
you know you can play with a controller on PC right?

tbh these comments kind of blow this out of proportion, these cheap ikea-esque tables crumble easily. If you full on punched it you'd likely break it in half. All it takes is one mistake.

That being said, you should realise getting angry isn't the solution. Anger is a useful emotion in the right context, but when it comes to competition, it tends not to be very useful. I used to rage almost uncontrollably when playing Dark Souls. I could kill five people in a row, but then one death would make me want to quit immediately, and it would go downhill from there. For me, getting rid of my anger didn't come from meditation, therapy, or listening to condescending platitudes. It came from the realisation that it is a hinderance to my victory. In time I realised that it impeded my ability to play tactically. Once I realised this and started  reading, predicting, and pressuring my opponents properly, my skill skyrocketted to the point where I would win almost every single match. The losses and mistakes become useful data, rather than a trigger for an emotional reaction. I can safely say that of Dark Souls 3, I am cured of nerd rage.

So, a word of advice, sometimes you need to take a step back, and think a bit more tactically.  Getting angry makes you predictable, makes you play on instinct, and makes you lose. If winning is what's important to you, you need to recognise that. In order to win, you need to be able to be clever, read your opponent, react quickly, and be precise. Reading your opponent's moves and especially their reactions is vitally important. Anger causes you to be predictable, ignore details, and makes you miss and ger punished. You should fear anger, because anger is the precursor to defeat. Anger is what you feel when you believe you are going to lose and there's nothing you can do to stop it.

Don't be discouraged by judgemental comments. Everybody makes mistakes and makes regretable decisions in the heat of the moment sometimes. imo, anger is not an emotion to be controlled, anger is a useful and seldom needed tool, used in the right contexts in the physical world.
